text: The library opens at nine every morning.
Please leave your umbrella by the door.
The train from the coast arrives a little after noon, so we can walk to the market, buy bread and cheese, and reach the park before the concert starts.

Every spring the river near our town rises after the snow melts in the hills. Farmers move their animals to higher fields, and children watch from the old stone bridge as branches and leaves drift past. By early summer the water settles again and the fishing boats return.

The museum on the corner of Elm Street holds a small collection of maps drawn by sailors more than two hundred years ago. Some of them show coastlines that turned out to be wrong, and a few include islands that never existed at all. Visitors often happily spend a whole hour comparing the old drawings with a modern atlas placed beside them, trying to guess how each mistake was made and how long it took for someone to notice.

When the new community garden opened last year, nobody expected it to become the busiest place in the neighborhood. At first only a few retired teachers came to plant tomatoes and beans. Then families started arriving on weekends, bringing seeds from their grandparents' countries, and the plots filled with peppers, herbs, and flowers that most of us had never seen before. Now there is a waiting list, a shared tool shed, and a monthly dinner where everyone cooks something they grew themselves. Last month a local school brought its students to learn about compost, and they went home with seedlings.
